content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) advises against Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination for children with symptomatic HIV infection or for individuals known or suspected to be infected with HIV if their risk of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection is minimal. 2. Globally, millions of individuals have received the BCG vaccine, and serious or long-term complications following vaccination are rare. Factors influencing adverse reaction rates include the BCG dose, vaccine strain, and method of administration. 3. Case reports suggest that BCG-related lymphadenitis, local ulceration, and disseminated BCG disease—occurring even years after vaccination—are more common in individuals with symptomatic HIV infection compared to those without HIV or with asymptomatic HIV infection. 4. Post-vaccination tuberculin reactivity induced by BCG vaccination can range from no induration to an induration of 19 mm at the skin test site. This reactivity diminishes over time and is unlikely to persist beyond 10 years after vaccination in the absence of M. 5. Weakened BCG-induced tuberculin reactivity may be boosted by administering a tuberculin skin test one week to one year after the initial post-vaccination test. Periodic skin testing may also prolong reactivity in vaccinated individuals. 6. The presence or size of a post-vaccination tuberculin skin-test reaction does not predict whether BCG vaccination will provide protection against tuberculosis (TB) disease. Additionally, the size of the reaction in a BCG-vaccinated person does not determine whether the reaction is due to M. tuberculosis infection or prior BCG vaccination. 7. A community-based survey in Quebec, Canada, found that the prevalence of tuberculin reactions of ≥10 mm induration in adolescents and young adults was similar among those vaccinated during infancy and those never vaccinated. However, individuals vaccinated after infancy had a significantly higher prevalence of such reactions compared to those never vaccinated, though the reaction size did not distinguish between reactions caused by BCG vaccination and those caused by M. tuberculosis infection. 8. tuberculosis infection. 9. Tuberculin skin testing is not contraindicated for BCG-vaccinated individuals, and their skin-test results can be used to support or exclude a diagnosis of M. tuberculosis infection. Preventive therapy should be considered for BCG-vaccinated individuals with a tuberculin skin-test reaction of ≥10 mm induration, especially if they have been in contact with an infectious TB case, were born or lived in a high TB prevalence country, or are exposed to high-risk populations. 10. Preventive therapy should also be considered for BCG-vaccinated individuals infected with HIV who are at risk for M. tuberculosis infection if they have a tuberculin skin-test reaction of ≥5 mm induration or are nonreactive to tuberculin due to potential anergy. 11. HIV infection can reduce responsiveness to tuberculin or other delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) antigens, a condition known as anergy, which may occur before the onset of HIV symptoms. Studies in Rwanda and Uganda have shown decreased tuberculin skin-test responses in HIV-infected children and women compared to uninfected controls. 12. A diagnosis of active TB disease should be considered in BCG-vaccinated individuals, regardless of their tuberculin skin-test results or HIV status, if they exhibit symptoms suggestive of TB, particularly if they have been recently exposed to infectious TB. 13. In the United States, the prevalence of M. tuberculosis infection and active TB disease varies across population segments, but the overall risk is low. The primary strategy for TB control is early identification and treatment of patients with active infectious TB to minimize transmission risk. 14. The secondary strategy involves identifying individuals with latent M. tuberculosis infection and, if indicated, using preventive therapy with isoniazid to prevent progression to active TB disease. Rifampin is used for preventive therapy in cases of isoniazid-resistant M. tuberculosis strains. 15. The use of BCG vaccination has been limited due to its uncertain effectiveness in preventing infectious TB forms and the interference of post-vaccination tuberculin reactivity with the management of individuals potentially infected with M. tuberculosis. BCG vaccination as a TB prevention strategy is reserved for select individuals meeting specific criteria. 16. A diagnosis of TB in a child is a sentinel event, indicating recent M. tuberculosis transmission within the community. Studies show that most children with TB acquire the infection from infected adults, often within the same household. 17. These findings highlight the importance of promptly reporting TB cases to public health authorities and initiating thorough contact investigations to identify children at risk for TB infection and disease. 18. The severity of active TB disease in childhood necessitates special efforts to protect children, particularly those under five years of age, from M. tuberculosis infection. This is achieved primarily by interrupting transmission through the early identification and treatment of individuals with infectious TB. 19. In adults, nonadherence to prescribed TB treatment can prolong infectiousness and increase M. tuberculosis transmission.
